title: Choosing state ownership boundaries
description: Learn how to decide which component or module should own a piece of state. Covers lifting state up, colocating state, and avoiding the common trap of prematurely lifting state to a global store.

data.text: State ownership is one of the most important architectural decisions in a React application. The component that owns a piece of state is the only component that can update it directly. Choosing the wrong owner leads to excessive prop drilling, unnecessary re-renders, or components that are impossible to reuse.
This lesson gives you a practical framework for deciding where state should live and how to move it when your initial choice turns out to be wrong.

If two sibling components need to share or coordinate state, the simplest fix is often to lift the state up to their nearest common ancestor. The ancestor holds the state and passes both the value and an updater function down as props.

data.title: Lifting state up to a common ancestor
data.content: The parent owns the selected item and tells each child what to render.

data.text: Not all shared state needs to live at the top of the tree. Colocating state means placing it as close as possible to the components that actually use it. Colocated state is easier to test, easier to delete, and does not force unrelated parts of the app to re-render.

data.title: When to colocate
items: A form and its submit button both need access to the same values.
A modal and the button that opens it share open/close state.
A dropdown menu and its trigger share expanded state.

data.title: Composition first
data.text: Before reaching for Context or a global store, ask whether you can solve the problem with composition. Wrapping components in a shared parent is often simpler and more explicit than introducing a new layer of indirection.

New React developers often reach for a global state manager because prop drilling feels tedious. In reality, prop drilling is only a problem when the intermediate components do not use the props themselves. If those components do need the props, passing them explicitly documents the data flow and keeps components reusable.

data.title: Prop drilling is not always a problem
data.content: A layout that receives theme and authentication state and passes them to children is perfectly readable.

data.text: Signs that state ownership is wrong

data.title: Warning signs
items: A component receives many props that it does not use, only to pass them further down.
Two unrelated features both depend on the same global state slice.
Tests require rendering a deep provider tree for simple unit tests.
A state change in one feature triggers unexpected re-renders in a different feature.

data.title: Exercise: refactor state ownership
data.description: A dashboard page places all form state, filter state, and table selection state in a top-level Context. Identify which pieces of state should be colocated closer to the components that use them and explain the benefit of moving them.
data.expectedOutcome: You should move form state into the form component, filter state into the toolbar, and table selection state into the table. Only truly global values such as theme or auth remain in Context.

data.title: Key takeaways
points: Start with local state and lift or colocate only when components actually need to share it.
Composition is often simpler and more explicit than Context.
Prop drilling is not inherently bad when intermediate components need the data.
Move state closer to the components that use it; global state is a last resort.
data.takeaway: Good state ownership keeps the data flow obvious, minimizes re-renders, and makes each component independently testable.
